// Builds draft.json for the "clinical" batch. Run: node build_draft.js "<output path>"
// Derived numbers come from calc.js (see calc_output.json in this folder).
const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');
const calc = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(path.join(__dirname, 'calc_output.json'), 'utf8'));

// ---- sources actually read (exact URLs fetched) ----
const S = {
  eanm: 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML',
  snm2006: 'https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/47/5/885.full.pdf',
  fdgLabel: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/5d05df4a-463e-4e66-9387-f3a842e20cd0.xml',
  radinfo: 'https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/pet',
  nhs: 'https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/pet-scan/',
  cruk: 'https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/tests-and-scans/pet-ct-scan',
  ucsf: 'https://radiology.ucsf.edu/patient-care/prepare/pet-ct',
  medline: 'https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003827.htm',
  unscear2020: 'https://www.unscear.org/unscear/uploads/documents/unscear-reports/UNSCEAR_2020_21_Report_Vol.I.pdf',
  unscear2008: 'https://www.unscear.org/unscear/uploads/documents/unscear-reports/UNSCEAR_2008_Report_Vol.I-CORR.pdf',
  epa: 'https://www.epa.gov/radiation/radiation-sources-and-doses',
  nrc: 'https://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/radiation/around-us/doses-daily-lives.html',
  brix: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=15809483&rettype=abstract&retmode=text',
  livechart: 'https://nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=all',
  dotmed: 'https://www.dotmed.com/news/story/50434',
  imv2025: 'https://www.scienceandmedicinegroup.com/resource/imv-pet-procedure-volumes-continue-strong-growth-trend/',
  gallach: 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC7476356/fullTextXML',
  lancet: 'https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8444235/',
  badawi: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=6424228',
  spencer: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=8729871',
  cherry: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=5750522',
  alberts: 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE%3A%22head-to-head%20intra-individual%20comparison%20of%20the%20Biograph%20Vision%20Quadra%22&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=3',
  jamar: 'https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/54/4/647',
  guedj: 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8803744/fullTextXML',
  sarcoid: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=23359660,28765228&rettype=abstract&retmode=text',
  netspot: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/b2b3be70-17d8-4093-896c-f1c54a2cf242.xml',
  pylarify: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/a00e5cbc-4fd5-4280-82ec-cd3498df4553.xml',
  locametz: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/8683b06e-4901-4526-89ad-23a8fe2d1331.xml',
  amyvid: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/bb5a5043-0f51-11df-8a39-0800200c9a66.xml',
  cardiogen: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/ee95aa18-9f2f-40eb-9b4c-583bea6f36bf.xml',
  ammonia: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/b1559f8a-1fc8-4a9e-b4f4-5e2efcb1f12c.xml'
};

const r = (x, n) => Number(x.toFixed(n));
const claims = [];
const add = (id, topic, statement, value, unit, range, sources, notes) =>
  claims.push({ id, topic, statement, value, unit, range, status: 'unverified', sources, notes });

// ---------------- 1. Preparation ----------------
add('prep-fasting', 'Draft claim 1: preparation (fasting)',
  'Before an FDG PET/CT scan for cancer, patients are asked not to eat or drink anything except plain water for at least 4 to 6 hours.',
  'at least 4 (European guideline); 4 to 6 (US guideline and FDA drug label)', 'hours',
  'European guideline (EANM 2015): at least 4 h before injection. US guideline (SNM 2006): at least 4 to 6 h. FDA label: 4 to 6 h. Many hospitals simply say 6 h (NHS, UCSF).',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006, S.fdgLabel, S.nhs, S.ucsf],
  'Draft confirmed. Drinking water is encouraged, not just allowed (EANM suggests about 1 L in the 2 h before injection). The fasting rule applies to cancer and brain scans; for the heart-viability scan the FDA label instead describes giving glucose (50 to 75 g) before injection, and scans for heart inflammation or infection may need a longer fast or a low-carbohydrate diet. Do not present 4 to 6 hours as a rule for every FDG scan.');

add('prep-blood-glucose', 'Draft claim 1: preparation (blood glucose)',
  'Staff check the blood sugar before the injection, and under European guidance the scan goes ahead if it is below 11 mmol/L (about 200 mg/dL).',
  '11 (about 200 mg/dL)', 'mmol/L',
  'EANM 2015: below 11 mmol/L (about 200 mg/dL) for clinical scans; 7 to 8.3 mmol/L (126 to 150 mg/dL) as the upper limit in research studies. SNM 2006: most institutions reschedule above 150 to 200 mg/dL.',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006, S.fdgLabel],
  'Draft confirmed. Unit check (calc.js): 11 mmol/L = ' + r(calc.glucose['11 mmol/L in mg/dL'], 0) + ' mg/dL and 200 mg/dL = ' + r(calc.glucose['200 mg/dL in mmol/L'], 1) + ' mmol/L, so "about 200 mg/dL" is a rounding. The reason: high blood sugar and insulin push FDG into muscle and reduce tumor uptake. EANM also says the level should not be too low (not below 4 mmol/L, about 70 mg/dL). Thresholds differ between hospitals, so keep the word "about" or name the guideline.');

add('prep-exercise', 'Draft claim 1: preparation (exercise)',
  'Patients are asked to avoid strenuous exercise for at least 6 hours, and preferably 24 hours, before the scan, because working muscles take up the tracer.',
  'at least 6, preferably 24', 'hours',
  'EANM 2015: at least 6 h, preferably 24 h. NHS: up to 24 hours. Cancer Research UK: 24 hours.',
  [S.eanm, S.nhs, S.cruk],
  'Draft said "about 24 hours"; the guideline wording is "at least 6 h ... and preferably for 24 h". Either form is safe if 24 hours is called the usual advice rather than a strict rule.');

// ---------------- 2. Uptake ----------------
add('uptake-time', 'Draft claim 2: uptake time',
  'After the injection the patient waits about 60 minutes before the scan starts, so that the tracer can spread through the body and collect in the tissues that use the most sugar.',
  '60', 'minutes',
  'EANM 2015: 60 min recommended, acceptable range 55 to 75 min. SNM 2006: images typically acquired more than 45 min after injection. FDA label: static images 30 to 100 min after injection. Brain-only scans can start earlier (30 to 50 min).',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006, S.fdgLabel, S.cruk, S.nhs],
  'Draft confirmed (60 min, 55 to 75 min). The 55 to 75 minute window comes from the European guideline and exists to keep uptake measurements (SUV) comparable between scans; it is not a safety limit. For a repeat scan of the same patient the guideline asks for the same waiting time to within 10 minutes.');

add('uptake-rest', 'Draft claim 2: what the patient does during uptake',
  'During the wait the patient sits or lies still in a warm, quiet room and is asked not to talk, because moving, talking and feeling cold all send tracer to muscle or brown fat instead of where the doctors want to look.',
  'seated or lying down, silent, kept warm', '',
  'Same advice in European and US guidelines; for brain scans the room is also dimly lit.',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006, S.radinfo],
  'Added detail, not in the draft. EANM: "the patient should remain seated or recumbent and silent" and "should be kept warm starting 30 to 60 min before the injection" to limit uptake in brown fat. Patients may use the toilet, and are asked to empty the bladder just before the scan.');

// ---------------- 3. Scanning ----------------
add('scan-ct-time', 'Draft claim 3: CT pass',
  'The CT pass comes first and takes less than two minutes.',
  'less than 2', 'minutes',
  'Depends on scanner and scan length; the X-ray beam itself is usually on for well under a minute on a modern multi-slice CT, but the only figure found in a patient-facing professional source is "less than two minutes".',
  [S.radinfo],
  'Draft said "under a minute". CORRECTED to "less than two minutes", the wording of RadiologyInfo.org (RSNA and ACR): "The CT scan takes less than two minutes." No authoritative source was found that states "under a minute" for the whole CT step, so the safer figure is used.');

add('scan-pet-time', 'Draft claim 3: PET pass',
  'The PET pass takes longer, usually about 15 to 30 minutes on a standard scanner, and the patient has to lie still for all of it.',
  '15 to 30', 'minutes',
  'SNM guideline 2006: 15 to 45 min for skull to mid-thigh. RadiologyInfo: PET scan 20 to 30 min, total scanning about 30 min. Cancer Research UK and UCSF: whole scan 30 to 45 min. NHS: 30 to 60 min. A 2021 study timed a routine scan on a current digital scanner (Siemens Biograph Vision 600) at 16 min for 106 cm of body coverage.',
  [S.snm2006, S.radinfo, S.cruk, S.ucsf, S.nhs, S.alberts],
  'Draft said "about 10 to 20 minutes on a modern scanner (older scanners 20 to 45 minutes)". CORRECTED: no authoritative source gives 10 minutes as typical for a standard scanner; the one measured modern figure found is 16 minutes, and current patient leaflets still say 20 to 45 minutes for the whole scan. The older figure is confirmed as 15 to 45 minutes (2006 guideline), not 20 to 45. Scan time depends on patient height and weight, injected activity and scanner sensitivity. Long total-body scanners are much faster (see total-body claims).');

add('scan-range', 'Draft claim 3: body coverage',
  'For most cancer scans the pictures run from the base of the skull to the middle of the thigh, which covers the places where most cancers spread.',
  'base of skull to mid-thigh', '',
  'Extended to the top of the head and to the feet for cancers that often involve the brain, scalp or legs (for example melanoma).',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006],
  'Draft confirmed. EANM calls this "torso imaging" and says it is "standard for both Europe and the US". Patients usually lie with arms raised above the head.');

add('visit-length', 'Draft claim 3: whole visit',
  'The whole visit takes about 2 hours, most of it spent waiting for the tracer to spread.',
  'about 2', 'hours',
  'Cancer Research UK: in the department for around 2 hours. UCSF: the entire procedure takes about two hours. RadiologyInfo: extra tests can lengthen the procedure to three hours.',
  [S.cruk, S.ucsf, S.radinfo],
  'Draft said "about 2 to 3 hours". Narrowed to "about 2 hours" because both sources that give a total say 2 hours; "2 to 3 hours" is still defensible as an allowance (RadiologyInfo mentions three hours when additional tests are done). Sum check: check-in and blood sugar test, about 60 min wait, about 30 min on the scanner.');

// ---------------- 4. Dose ----------------
add('fdg-injected-activity', 'Draft claim 4: injected activity',
  'A typical adult FDG injection contains 185 to 370 MBq of fluorine-18 (5 to 10 millicuries).',
  '185 to 370', 'MBq',
  'FDA label: 5 to 10 mCi (185 to 370 MBq) for adults. European practice scales the activity to body weight and scan time and is often lower. National survey averages collected by UNSCEAR run from 280 to 400 MBq.',
  [S.fdgLabel, S.eanm, S.unscear2020],
  'Draft range confirmed against the FDA label. Unit check (calc.js): 185 MBq = 5 mCi, 370 MBq = 10 mCi. Newer, more sensitive scanners allow lower activities; UNSCEAR notes French units with time-of-flight scanners averaged 3.4 MBq/kg against 4.6 MBq/kg without.');

add('fdg-dose-coefficient', 'Draft claim 4: FDG effective dose',
  'The tracer gives an adult an effective dose of about 0.019 mSv for every MBq injected, so a 185 to 370 MBq injection gives about 3.5 to 7 mSv.',
  '0.019 (so 3.5 to 7.0 mSv for 185 to 370 MBq)', 'mSv/MBq',
  'Adult value. Children get more per MBq (EANM table: 0.024 at 15 years, 0.037 at 10 years, 0.056 at 5 years, 0.095 at 1 year) but are given less activity.',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006],
  'Draft confirmed. Recomputed (calc.js): 185 x 0.019 = ' + calc.fdgDose_mSv['185 MBq'] + ' mSv; 370 x 0.019 = ' + calc.fdgDose_mSv['370 MBq'] + ' mSv. The coefficient is quoted from ICRP Publication 106 by the EANM guideline ("1.9 x 10^-2 mSv/MBq ... i.e. about 3.5 mSv for an administered activity of 185 MBq") and the same 0.019 appears in the SNM 2006 guideline citing ICRP Publication 80. The ICRP publications themselves were not opened (paywalled); the value was read from the two guidelines that quote them. The organ that receives the most is the bladder wall, which is why patients are told to drink and urinate often.');

add('ct-dose', 'Draft claim 4: CT part of the dose',
  'The CT part adds anywhere from about 1 mSv for the faintest scan used only to correct the PET picture, to 10 to 20 mSv or more for a full diagnostic CT; the low-dose whole-body CT used in most scans added about 3 to 9 mSv in national surveys.',
  '1 to 20 (low-dose protocols in surveys: 2.9 to 8.6)', 'mSv',
  'EANM 2015: "The effective CT dose ranges from 1 to 20 mSv and may be even higher". UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Table D19 low-dose CT component: 2.9 (Germany 2004), 5.9, 6, 6.3, 6.5, 8.2, 8.6 mSv; 13.3 mSv where diagnostic CT was mainly used (Russian Federation 2014 to 2017).',
  [S.eanm, S.unscear2020],
  'Draft said "roughly 1 to 3 mSv for a low-dose CT". CORRECTED: survey data show that the "low-dose" CT actually used in whole-body PET/CT usually adds about 3 to 9 mSv; about 1 mSv is the bottom of the EANM range and applies only to very low-dose attenuation-correction scans. The "up to 10 to 20 mSv for a full diagnostic CT" part is consistent with EANM. The SNM 2006 guideline gave an even wider theoretical range (about 5 to 80 mSv) for older protocols; not recommended for the site.');

add('total-dose', 'Draft claim 4: total dose',
  'A whole-body FDG PET/CT scan typically gives a total effective dose of about 10 to 19 mSv, with about 14 mSv a common figure; older scans that included a full diagnostic CT reached about 25 mSv.',
  'about 14 to 15 typical; 10 to 19 in national surveys; about 25 with full diagnostic CT (2005 German study)', 'mSv',
  'UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Table D19 national totals: 9.9, 12.2, 12.7, 14.1, 14.2, 14.3 and 18.6 mSv (10 to 13 mSv for the Russian Federation 2011 to 2013). UNSCEAR text: "a total procedure dose of 14 mSv is not uncommon" and "a typical effective dose of 15 mSv per procedure". Brix et al. 2005 (four German hospitals, diagnostic contrast CT included): about 25 mSv. Arithmetic limits from the guideline ranges: ' + r(calc.total.total_min, 1) + ' to ' + r(calc.total.total_max, 0) + ' mSv.',
  [S.unscear2020, S.brix, S.eanm],
  'Draft said "about 10 to 25 mSv". Refined: the range is right as an outer envelope, but the upper end (25 mSv) comes from a 2005 study on early scanners with full diagnostic CT, and current survey averages sit between 10 and 19 mSv. Each UNSCEAR table row was re-added (PET part + CT part = total) in calc.js and all seven agree. Newer scanners and total-body scanners can go well below 10 mSv. Effective dose is a population-average risk indicator, not a measured dose to one patient; avoid wording that implies precision.');

add('background-world', 'Draft claim 4: natural background, world',
  'For comparison, natural background radiation gives the average person in the world about 2.4 mSv every year.',
  '2.4', 'mSv per year',
  'Typical range 1 to 13 mSv per year depending on where a person lives; sizeable population groups receive 10 to 20 mSv. Components: radon 1.26, ground 0.48, cosmic 0.39, food and drink 0.29 (sum 2.42).',
  [S.unscear2008],
  'Draft confirmed against the UNSCEAR 2008 Report, Volume I (table of average annual doses: "Total natural 2.4", typical range "1 to 13"; Annex B: "worldwide average annual exposure to natural radiation sources remains at 2.4 mSv").');

add('background-usa', 'Draft claim 4: natural background, USA',
  'In the United States the average person receives about 3.1 mSv a year from natural background radiation, and about 6.2 mSv a year in total once medical scans are included.',
  '3.1 natural; 6.2 total', 'mSv per year',
  'The US natural figure is higher than the world average mainly because of radon. Both figures are from NCRP Report No. 160 (2009, data for 2006).',
  [S.epa, S.nrc],
  'Draft said "about 3 mSv per year in the USA"; confirmed and made exact. EPA: "the average annual radiation dose per person in the U.S. is 6.2 millisieverts (620 millirem)" (source NCRP Report No. 160) and about 48 percent of it comes from medical procedures. NRC: "about 0.62 rem (620 millirem) each year. Half of this dose comes from natural background radiation." Half of 6.2 = ' + calc.background.us_natural_from_half_of_6_2 + ' mSv (calc.js). The NRC page blocked direct download and was read through a fetch tool summary; the EPA page was read directly. NCRP Report 160 itself was not opened (paywalled). A later NCRP report (No. 184, 2019) lowered the medical part for 2016; it was not read, so do not quote a newer total.');

add('dose-in-background-years', 'Draft claim 4: comparison of scan dose with background',
  'A 14 mSv PET/CT scan is roughly what a person receives from natural background radiation in about 6 years at the world average rate, or about 4 to 5 years at the United States rate.',
  '5.8 (world, 2.4 mSv/y); 4.5 (USA, 3.1 mSv/y)', 'years of natural background',
  'For the 10 to 19 mSv survey range: about 4 to 8 years at 2.4 mSv per year. For the FDG part alone (3.5 to 7 mSv): about 1.5 to 3 years.',
  [S.unscear2020, S.unscear2008, S.epa],
  'Derived in calc.js: 14 / 2.4 = ' + calc.background.years_world_for['14 mSv'] + ' years; 14 / 3.1 = ' + calc.background.years_us_for['14 mSv'] + ' years; 10 / 2.4 = ' + calc.background.years_world_for['10 mSv'] + '; 7 / 2.4 = ' + calc.background.years_world_for['7 mSv'] + '; 3.5 / 2.4 = ' + calc.background.years_world_for['3.5 mSv'] + '. This comparison is this project\'s own arithmetic, not a quoted figure, and it compares whole-body averages only.');

// ---------------- 5. Decay and aftercare ----------------
add('f18-decay-11h', 'Draft claim 5: how fast the radioactivity disappears',
  'Fluorine-18 loses half of its radioactivity every 110 minutes, so 11 hours after the injection (six half-lives) only about 1.5% is left from decay alone, and the body removes more through urine.',
  '1.55 (1/64 = 1.56 if the half-life is rounded to 110 min)', '% remaining after 11 hours',
  'Half-life 109.77 min (IAEA nuclear data; FDA labels print 109.7 or 109.8 min). Remaining by decay alone: 68% after 1 h, 47% after 2 h, 22% after 4 h, 10% after 6 h, 3.3% after 9 h, 1.1% after 12 h, 0.011% after 24 h.',
  [S.livechart, S.fdgLabel],
  'Draft arithmetic confirmed (calc.js): 660 min / 109.77 min = ' + r(calc.f18.halfLives_in_11h, 3) + ' half-lives, leaving ' + r(calc.f18.remaining_after_11h_pct_T109_77, 2) + '%; with a rounded 110 min half-life it is exactly 6 half-lives and 1/64 = ' + calc.f18.remaining_after_11h_pct_T110 + '%. Either way "about 1.5%" (or "about 1/64") is correct. Decay alone reaches 1% after ' + r(calc.f18.hours_to_1pct, 1) + ' hours. The body also excretes FDG: the FDA label reports about 20.6% of the dose in the bladder 2 hours after injection, so the true amount left in the body is lower than these decay-only figures. MedlinePlus says the radiation "is gone from your body in about 2 to 10 hours", which is looser than the arithmetic; prefer the calculated wording.');

add('after-scan-advice', 'Draft claim 5: advice after the scan',
  'After the scan patients can eat normally, are told to drink plenty of water and empty the bladder often, and are usually asked to avoid long, close contact with babies, young children and pregnant people for the rest of the day.',
  'rest of the day (UK patient advice); 9 to 12 hours appears in guidance for breastfeeding mothers', '',
  'NHS: avoid spending a long time or having close contact with young children or anyone who is pregnant, "such as for the rest of the day". Cancer Research UK: "for the rest of the day". FDA label: urinate as soon as the scan is finished and as often as possible for at least one hour. Local rules differ and some centers give no restriction.',
  [S.nhs, S.cruk, S.fdgLabel, S.radinfo],
  'Draft said "for some hours"; confirmed, and the two UK patient sources give "the rest of the day". No US patient-facing source with a specific number of hours for general contact was found, so the statement uses "usually" and "the rest of the day". Drinking water matters because the bladder wall is the organ that receives the highest dose.');

// ---------------- 6. Uses ----------------
add('uses-cancer', 'Draft claim 6: main uses (cancer)',
  'Most PET/CT scans are done for cancer: to find a tumor, to see how far it has spread, to check whether treatment is working and to look for cancer that has come back.',
  'about 9 in 10 scans', '',
  'United States 2019 (IMV survey): heart scans 8% and brain scans 3% of PET volume, leaving about 89% that is almost all cancer. UNSCEAR: oncology is "more than 90% of all PET procedures in most countries". A Canadian survey cited by a Lancet Oncology Commission found 80.2%.',
  [S.fdgLabel, S.eanm, S.dotmed, S.unscear2020, S.lancet, S.cruk],
  'Draft "the large majority of scans" confirmed. The 89% is a subtraction (100 - 8 - 3, calc.js), not a figure stated by IMV, and the IMV numbers were read from a trade-press report of the paid survey. Safest site wording: "about 9 in 10" or "the large majority". The FDA label lists the cancers in the approval studies: lung, colorectal, pancreatic, breast, thyroid, melanoma, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.');

add('uses-heart', 'Draft claim 6: main uses (heart)',
  'In the heart, FDG PET shows whether weakened heart muscle is still alive and could recover if its blood supply is restored, and it is used to look for inflammation such as cardiac sarcoidosis; other PET tracers measure blood flow to the heart muscle.',
  'viability; inflammation (cardiac sarcoidosis); blood flow with rubidium-82 or nitrogen-13 ammonia', '',
  'About 8% of US PET scans in 2019 were heart scans, mostly blood-flow (perfusion) scans.',
  [S.fdgLabel, S.jamar, S.sarcoid, S.cardiogen, S.ammonia, S.dotmed],
  'Draft confirmed. FDA label wording for the heart: "identification of left ventricular myocardium with residual glucose metabolism and reversible loss of systolic function in patients with coronary artery disease and left ventricular dysfunction". Sarcoidosis is listed as a major indication in the EANM/SNMMI inflammation guideline (read through a fetch tool summary), and a joint SNMMI-ASNC consensus document (2017) covers FDG PET/CT in cardiac sarcoid; only its title and citation were read. Note that most heart PET scans use perfusion tracers, not FDG.');

add('uses-brain', 'Draft claim 6: main uses (brain)',
  'In the brain, FDG PET helps tell different types of dementia apart by showing which regions use less sugar than normal, and helps find the starting point of seizures in people with epilepsy who are being considered for surgery.',
  'dementia; epilepsy (pre-surgical)', '',
  'About 3% of US PET scans in 2019 were brain scans. Other uses in the European brain guideline: movement disorders such as atypical parkinsonism, encephalitis, brain tumors.',
  [S.guedj, S.fdgLabel, S.dotmed],
  'Draft confirmed. Epilepsy is an FDA-labeled use ("regions of abnormal glucose metabolism associated with foci of epileptic seizures"); dementia is covered by the EANM brain guideline (2022) but is not in the FDA FDG label. Amyloid tracers such as florbetapir are a separate kind of brain PET scan (see tracer claims).');

add('uses-infection-inflammation', 'Draft claim 6: main uses (infection and inflammation)',
  'Because infected and inflamed tissue also uses extra sugar, FDG PET/CT is used to look for hidden infections, the cause of a long unexplained fever, inflamed blood vessels and sarcoidosis.',
  'sarcoidosis; bone and spine infection; fever of unknown origin; spread of infection in the blood; vasculitis', '',
  'Major indications listed in the 2013 EANM/SNMMI guideline: sarcoidosis; peripheral bone osteomyelitis; suspected spinal infection; fever of unknown origin; metastatic infection and high-risk bacteremia; primary evaluation of vasculitides such as giant cell arteritis.',
  [S.jamar, S.eanm],
  'Draft confirmed. The guideline page blocked direct download and was read through a fetch tool summary that quoted the list; treat the exact list as needing a second look before quoting it verbatim. This use is not in the FDA FDG label (off-label in the US) but is established in guidelines. The same sugar uptake is why infection and inflammation can be mistaken for cancer on a scan.');

// ---------------- 7. Scale ----------------
add('scale-usa-scans', 'Draft claim 7: scans per year, USA',
  'In the United States about 2.2 million PET scans were done in 2019, the highest yearly total recorded up to then.',
  '2,200,800 (2019)', 'scans per year',
  'IMV reported growth of about 6% a year from 2013 to 2019 and, in a later report, a 12.2% rise in 2024 over 2023, so the current yearly total is higher than 2.2 million, but no later absolute figure was found in an open source.',
  [S.dotmed, S.imv2025],
  'Draft said "about 2 million"; CORRECTED to 2.2 million with the year 2019. The figure is an estimate from a commercial survey (IMV 2020 PET Imaging Market Summary Report), read as reported by DOTmed HealthCare Business News on March 11, 2020, not from the paid report itself. It counts clinical PET scans on fixed and mobile PET, PET/CT and PET/MR systems. The 2024 growth figure comes from IMV\'s own summary of its 2025 report. Do not extrapolate a 2024 or 2025 total on the site.');

add('scale-usa-scanners', 'Draft claim 7: scanners, USA',
  'The United States has roughly 1,700 PET scanners, about 5 for every million people, and about 2,370 hospitals and clinics offered PET scans in 2019, four in ten of them using a mobile scanner that visits on a truck.',
  '1,680 PET systems (5.2 per million), of which 1,596 PET/CT; 2,370 sites in 2019', 'scanners; sites',
  'UNSCEAR Global Survey (data submitted for the 2009 to 2018 assessment; the table does not give the exact year): United States 1,680 PET systems, 5.2 per million; Denmark 7.4 per million. IMV 2019: 2,370 sites, 60% with fixed units and 40% served by mobile PET.',
  [S.unscear2020, S.dotmed],
  'The draft gave no number. The scanner count is from UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Report, Annex A, Table D33; its exact survey year is not printed, so say "in the 2010s". 1,680 / 5.2 implies a population of ' + r(calc.scale.implied_us_population_millions, 0) + ' million, consistent with 2015 to 2016. Site split recomputed: 60% of 2,370 = ' + r(calc.scale.us_fixed_sites, 0) + ' fixed, 40% = ' + r(calc.scale.us_mobile_sites, 0) + ' mobile (calc.js). "On a truck" is this project\'s plain description of a mobile PET service; the source says mobile services "stop at their facilities for several days each month".');

add('scale-world-scans', 'Draft claim 7: scans per year, worldwide',
  'Nobody keeps an exact worldwide count, but United Nations figures suggest several million PET scans a year, roughly 7 million, with about a third of them in the United States.',
  'about 6.8 million (derived: 17% of 40 million), period 2009 to 2018', 'scans per year',
  'Very uncertain. UNSCEAR gives its nuclear medicine totals an uncertainty of tens of percent, and the 17% PET share comes from the countries that answered its survey (range 1% to 67% between countries).',
  [S.unscear2020],
  'The draft gave no number. This is a DERIVED estimate, not a quoted one: UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Report (Annex A) assesses "the total number of procedures worldwide in diagnostic nuclear medicine (including PET)" as 40 million a year for 2009 to 2018 and says PET procedures "now represent 17% of all nuclear medicine procedures"; 40 million x 0.17 = ' + r(calc.scale.world_pet_estimate / 1e6, 1) + ' million (calc.js). The US 2019 figure (2.2 million) would be ' + r(calc.scale.us_share_of_world_estimate_pct, 0) + '% of that. Market-research sites quote 3 to 5 million, which looks too low against the US figure alone and was not used. If the site wants zero risk, say "several million a year" and drop the specific 7 million.');

add('scale-world-scanners', 'Draft claim 7: scanners, worldwide',
  'PET scanners are spread very unevenly: the International Atomic Energy Agency found about one PET/CT scanner for every 600,000 people in high-income countries, against one for every 167 million people in low-income countries.',
  'no authoritative worldwide total found; 1 per about 601,000 people (high income) to 1 per about 166,667,000 (low income)', 'people per PET/CT scanner',
  'IAEA IMAGINE database as analyzed by Gallach et al. 2020: 601,000 (high income), 3,484,000 (upper-middle), 10,000,000 (lower-middle), 166,667,000 (low income). UNSCEAR: 7 of 49 surveyed countries had no PET at all. Lancet Oncology Commission (IMAGINE data): mean 3.6 PET scanners per million people in high-income countries, 0.3 in upper-middle-income countries.',
  [S.gallach, S.unscear2020, S.lancet],
  'NOT RESOLVED: no primary or authoritative source with a worldwide total number of PET or PET/CT scanners could be read. The IAEA IMAGINE database holds country figures but only as an interactive dashboard that could not be downloaded, and its data date from about 2019 to 2020. Do not print a world total on the site. The per-person figures are from an IAEA-authored paper (Medical Science Monitor 2020) and are averages by World Bank income group. The Lancet Commission table has internal oddities (the stated mean exceeds the stated upper quartile), so quote it with care or not at all.');

// ---------------- 8. Total-body PET ----------------
add('totalbody-length', 'Draft claim 8: total-body PET, length',
  'The uEXPLORER scanner, built by a team at the University of California, Davis with United Imaging Healthcare in Shanghai, has a detector tunnel 194 cm long, enough to image the whole body of more than 99% of adults at once.',
  '194', 'cm (axial field of view)',
  'A standard PET/CT scanner covers about 15 to 30 cm at a time (the one in the 2021 comparison study covers 26.3 cm) and moves the patient through in steps. Another long scanner, the Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra, covers 106 cm.',
  [S.badawi, S.spencer, S.alberts],
  'Draft confirmed: "The 194-cm axial field of view of the EXPLORER PET/CT scanner is sufficient to cover, for the first time, the entire human adult body in a single acquisition in more than 99% of the population" (Badawi et al., J Nucl Med 2019). The first human studies were published in 2019; Spencer et al. 2021 call uEXPLORER "the first commercially available total-body PET scanner". Only the abstracts and author affiliations of these papers were read (full text not open through the API). 194 / 26.3 = ' + r(calc.explorer.ratio_to_26_3cm, 1) + ' times the coverage of that standard scanner (calc.js). The "15 to 30 cm" for standard scanners is general knowledge and should be checked against the instrumentation batch.');

add('totalbody-sensitivity', 'Draft claim 8: total-body PET, sensitivity',
  'Because its detectors surround the whole body, a total-body scanner catches far more of the gamma rays, and its designers calculated a gain of about 40 times for whole-body imaging compared with a standard scanner.',
  'about 40 (whole body); about 4 to 5 (single organ)', 'times the effective sensitivity',
  'The factor of about 40 is a design estimate published in 2018 before the scanner was finished. The measured sensitivity of the finished scanner is 174 kcps/MBq (NEMA NU 2-2018 test).',
  [S.cherry, S.spencer],
  'Draft confirmed with a caveat. Source wording (Cherry et al., J Nucl Med 2018): "by increasing the geometric coverage to encompass the entire body, sensitivity can be increased by a factor of about 40 for total-body imaging or a factor of about 4 to 5 for imaging a single organ such as the brain or heart". Present it as "about 40 times" or "up to about 40 times" for whole-body scans and say it is a calculated figure; do not say "40 times better pictures". Abstracts only were read.');

add('totalbody-fast-low-dose', 'Draft claim 8: total-body PET, speed and dose',
  'The extra sensitivity can be spent in different ways: the first human studies showed usable whole-body pictures from scans of about 1 minute or less, or from an injection of only 25 MBq, less than a tenth of a usual dose.',
  'about 1 minute or less; 25 MBq or less', '',
  'Initial case studies (2019), not routine practice. A 2021 patient study on a 106 cm scanner matched a 16-minute standard scan in under 2 minutes.',
  [S.badawi, S.alberts],
  'Draft confirmed. Source wording (Badawi et al. 2019): "the sensitivity gain can be used to acquire diagnostic PET images with very small amounts of activity in the field of view (25 MBq, 0.7 mCi or less), with very short acquisition times (about 1 min or less) or at later time points". The authors call this "initial evidence". Arithmetic (calc.js): 25 MBq x 0.019 = ' + calc.fdgDose_mSv['25 MBq'] + ' mSv from the tracer, and 370 / 25 = ' + calc.explorer.dose_ratio_370_over_25 + ', so "less than a tenth of a usual dose" holds for usual doses above 250 MBq; against the lowest label dose (185 MBq) it is about one seventh, so "a small fraction" is the wording that is true in every case. The same scanner can also film the tracer moving through the whole body with frames as short as 1 second.');

add('tracer-ga68-dotatate', 'Draft claim 9: other tracers (Ga-68 DOTATATE)',
  'Gallium-68 DOTATATE (half-life 68 minutes) sticks to somatostatin receptors and is used to find neuroendocrine tumors.',
  '67.71', 'minutes (half-life of gallium-68)',
  'Labels round to 68 min. Gallium-68 comes from a germanium-68 generator (half-life 270.93 days), so no cyclotron is needed on site.',
  [S.netspot, S.livechart],
  'Confirmed against the NETSPOT label: "indicated for use with positron emission tomography (PET) for localization of somatostatin receptor positive neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) in adult and pediatric patients"; label states initial US approval 2016. Half-life from IAEA nuclear data (4062.6 s).');

add('tracer-psma', 'Draft claim 9: other tracers (PSMA agents)',
  'PSMA tracers, made with either gallium-68 (half-life 68 minutes) or fluorine-18 (half-life 110 minutes), stick to a protein on prostate cancer cells and are used to find prostate cancer that has spread or come back.',
  'Ga-68 gozetotide (PSMA-11): 67.71 min; F-18 piflufolastat (DCFPyL): 109.77 min', 'minutes (half-life)',
  'US labels give initial approval years of 2020 for gallium Ga 68 gozetotide (PSMA-11) and 2021 for piflufolastat F 18 (Pylarify).',
  [S.locametz, S.pylarify, S.livechart],
  'Confirmed against the LOCAMETZ and PYLARIFY labels: PET "of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positive lesions in men with prostate cancer" with suspected metastasis before first treatment or suspected recurrence based on a rising PSA. PSMA is prostate-specific membrane antigen. Avoid "first PSMA tracer" claims on the site; the FDA announcement of the 2020 approval could not be opened.');

add('tracer-florbetapir', 'Draft claim 9: other tracers (F-18 florbetapir)',
  'Fluorine-18 florbetapir (half-life 110 minutes) sticks to amyloid plaques in the brain and is used when doctors are investigating Alzheimer\'s disease and other causes of memory loss.',
  '109.77', 'minutes (half-life of fluorine-18)',
  'Other amyloid tracers with the same isotope exist (florbetaben, flutemetamol); they were not checked in this batch.',
  [S.amyvid, S.livechart],
  'Confirmed against the AMYVID label: PET "of the brain to estimate amyloid beta neuritic plaque density in adults with cognitive impairment" for evaluation of Alzheimer\'s disease and other causes of cognitive decline, and for selecting patients for amyloid-directed therapy; label states initial US approval 2012. A positive scan shows plaques; it does not by itself diagnose Alzheimer\'s disease.');

add('tracer-rb82', 'Draft claim 9: other tracers (Rb-82)',
  'Rubidium-82 has a half-life of only 75 seconds, is drawn fresh from a generator next to the scanner, and is used to map blood flow to the heart muscle at rest and under stress.',
  '75.45', 'seconds (half-life of rubidium-82; 1.2575 minutes)',
  'Label rounds to 75 seconds. The generator holds strontium-82 (half-life about 25 days).',
  [S.cardiogen, S.livechart],
  'Confirmed against the CardioGen-82 label: PET "of the myocardium under rest or pharmacologic stress conditions to evaluate regional myocardial perfusion in adult patients with suspected or existing coronary artery disease"; label states initial US approval 1989. After 10 minutes only ' + calc.halfLives['Rb-82'].pct_left_after_10min + '% of the rubidium-82 is left (calc.js).');

add('tracer-n13-ammonia', 'Draft claim 9: other tracers (N-13 ammonia)',
  'Nitrogen-13 ammonia has a half-life of about 10 minutes, so it must be made in a cyclotron close to the scanner, and it is also used to map blood flow to the heart muscle.',
  '9.965', 'minutes (half-life of nitrogen-13)',
  'Label rounds to 9.96 minutes.',
  [S.ammonia, S.livechart],
  'Confirmed against an Ammonia N 13 Injection label: "diagnostic PET imaging of the myocardium under rest or pharmacologic stress conditions to evaluate myocardial perfusion in patients with suspected or existing coronary artery disease". The label read prints "Initial U.S. Approval: 2007"; do not use this as the date ammonia PET began, since the tracer was in research use decades earlier. "Close to the scanner" is this project\'s inference from the 10-minute half-life (half is gone every 10 minutes: ' + calc.halfLives['N-13'].pct_left_after_60min + '% left after an hour, calc.js).');

// ---------------- 10. Comfort and precautions ----------------
add('scan-painless', 'Draft claim 10: comfort',
  'The scan itself does not hurt; the only pain is the brief sting of the needle for the injection, and the hardest part for most people is lying still.',
  'painless apart from the injection', '',
  '',
  [S.medline, S.radinfo, S.cruk],
  'Draft confirmed. MedlinePlus: "A PET scan causes no pain" and "You may feel a sharp sting when the needle with the tracer is placed into your vein". RadiologyInfo: "Except for intravenous injections, most nuclear medicine procedures are painless." Cancer Research UK: "The scan is painless but can be uncomfortable because you have to stay still." Rare problems mentioned by these sources: tracer leaking outside the vein, and rare allergic reactions. People who fear closed spaces can be given a calming medicine.');

add('precaution-pregnancy', 'Draft claim 10: pregnancy',
  'Patients are asked to tell the staff if they are or might be pregnant, because the tracer crosses the placenta and the unborn baby would receive some radiation, so the scan is done in pregnancy only when doctors judge that the benefit outweighs that risk.',
  'benefit weighed against risk case by case', '',
  'Cancer Research UK: "Pregnant women should only have the scan in an emergency." EANM: "a clinical decision is necessary in which the benefits are weighed against the possible harm".',
  [S.fdgLabel, S.eanm, S.cruk, S.medline, S.radinfo],
  'FDA label: published reports "describe Fludeoxyglucose F 18 Injection crossing the placenta with uptake by the fetus"; "All radiopharmaceuticals have the potential to cause fetal harm depending on the fetal stage of development and the magnitude of the radiation dose"; published studies "have not identified a risk of drug-associated major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes". The CT part adds further dose to the baby. Keep the wording neutral: pregnancy is a reason for caution, not an absolute ban.');

add('precaution-breastfeeding', 'Draft claim 10: breastfeeding',
  'Breastfeeding mothers get specific instructions, which differ between countries: the United States drug label says to pump and discard milk and avoid close contact with the baby for 9 hours after the injection, while European guidance says breastfeeding need not stop but close contact should be limited for 12 hours.',
  '9 (US FDA label); 12 (European guideline, contact only)', 'hours',
  'NHS: "not breastfeeding for a few hours afterwards". RadiologyInfo: pump milk ahead of time to use until the tracer is gone.',

// Builds draft.json for the "clinical" batch. Run: node build_draft.js "<output path>"
// Derived numbers come from calc.js (see calc_output.json in this folder).
const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');
const calc = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(path.join(__dirname, 'calc_output.json'), 'utf8'));

// ---- sources actually read (exact URLs fetched) ----
const S = {
  eanm: 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4315529/fullTextXML',
  snm2006: 'https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/47/5/885.full.pdf',
  fdgLabel: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/5d05df4a-463e-4e66-9387-f3a842e20cd0.xml',
  radinfo: 'https://www.radiologyinfo.org/en/info/pet',
  nhs: 'https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/pet-scan/',
  cruk: 'https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/tests-and-scans/pet-ct-scan',
  ucsf: 'https://radiology.ucsf.edu/patient-care/prepare/pet-ct',
  medline: 'https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003827.htm',
  unscear2020: 'https://www.unscear.org/unscear/uploads/documents/unscear-reports/UNSCEAR_2020_21_Report_Vol.I.pdf',
  unscear2008: 'https://www.unscear.org/unscear/uploads/documents/unscear-reports/UNSCEAR_2008_Report_Vol.I-CORR.pdf',
  epa: 'https://www.epa.gov/radiation/radiation-sources-and-doses',
  nrc: 'https://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/radiation/around-us/doses-daily-lives.html',
  brix: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=15809483&rettype=abstract&retmode=text',
  livechart: 'https://nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=all',
  dotmed: 'https://www.dotmed.com/news/story/50434',
  imv2025: 'https://www.scienceandmedicinegroup.com/resource/imv-pet-procedure-volumes-continue-strong-growth-trend/',
  gallach: 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC7476356/fullTextXML',
  lancet: 'https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8444235/',
  badawi: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=6424228',
  spencer: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=8729871',
  cherry: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pmc&id=5750522',
  alberts: 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE%3A%22head-to-head%20intra-individual%20comparison%20of%20the%20Biograph%20Vision%20Quadra%22&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=3',
  jamar: 'https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/54/4/647',
  guedj: 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8803744/fullTextXML',
  sarcoid: 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=23359660,28765228&rettype=abstract&retmode=text',
  netspot: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/b2b3be70-17d8-4093-896c-f1c54a2cf242.xml',
  pylarify: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/a00e5cbc-4fd5-4280-82ec-cd3498df4553.xml',
  locametz: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/8683b06e-4901-4526-89ad-23a8fe2d1331.xml',
  amyvid: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/bb5a5043-0f51-11df-8a39-0800200c9a66.xml',
  cardiogen: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/ee95aa18-9f2f-40eb-9b4c-583bea6f36bf.xml',
  ammonia: 'https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/services/v2/spls/b1559f8a-1fc8-4a9e-b4f4-5e2efcb1f12c.xml'
};

const r = (x, n) => Number(x.toFixed(n));
const claims = [];
const add = (id, topic, statement, value, unit, range, sources, notes) =>
  claims.push({ id, topic, statement, value, unit, range, status: 'unverified', sources, notes });

// ---------------- 1. Preparation ----------------
add('prep-fasting', 'Draft claim 1: preparation (fasting)',
  'Before an FDG PET/CT scan for cancer, patients are asked not to eat or drink anything except plain water for at least 4 to 6 hours.',
  'at least 4 (European guideline); 4 to 6 (US guideline and FDA drug label)', 'hours',
  'European guideline (EANM 2015): at least 4 h before injection. US guideline (SNM 2006): at least 4 to 6 h. FDA label: 4 to 6 h. Many hospitals simply say 6 h (NHS, UCSF).',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006, S.fdgLabel, S.nhs, S.ucsf],
  'Draft confirmed. Drinking water is encouraged, not just allowed (EANM suggests about 1 L in the 2 h before injection). The fasting rule applies to cancer and brain scans; for the heart-viability scan the FDA label instead describes giving glucose (50 to 75 g) before injection, and scans for heart inflammation or infection may need a longer fast or a low-carbohydrate diet. Do not present 4 to 6 hours as a rule for every FDG scan.');

add('prep-blood-glucose', 'Draft claim 1: preparation (blood glucose)',
  'Staff check the blood sugar before the injection, and under European guidance the scan goes ahead if it is below 11 mmol/L (about 200 mg/dL).',
  '11 (about 200 mg/dL)', 'mmol/L',
  'EANM 2015: below 11 mmol/L (about 200 mg/dL) for clinical scans; 7 to 8.3 mmol/L (126 to 150 mg/dL) as the upper limit in research studies. SNM 2006: most institutions reschedule above 150 to 200 mg/dL.',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006, S.fdgLabel],
  'Draft confirmed. Unit check (calc.js): 11 mmol/L = ' + r(calc.glucose['11 mmol/L in mg/dL'], 0) + ' mg/dL and 200 mg/dL = ' + r(calc.glucose['200 mg/dL in mmol/L'], 1) + ' mmol/L, so "about 200 mg/dL" is a rounding. The reason: high blood sugar and insulin push FDG into muscle and reduce tumor uptake. EANM also says the level should not be too low (not below 4 mmol/L, about 70 mg/dL). Thresholds differ between hospitals, so keep the word "about" or name the guideline.');

add('prep-exercise', 'Draft claim 1: preparation (exercise)',
  'Patients are asked to avoid strenuous exercise for at least 6 hours, and preferably 24 hours, before the scan, because working muscles take up the tracer.',
  'at least 6, preferably 24', 'hours',
  'EANM 2015: at least 6 h, preferably 24 h. NHS: up to 24 hours. Cancer Research UK: 24 hours.',
  [S.eanm, S.nhs, S.cruk],
  'Draft said "about 24 hours"; the guideline wording is "at least 6 h ... and preferably for 24 h". Either form is safe if 24 hours is called the usual advice rather than a strict rule.');

// ---------------- 2. Uptake ----------------
add('uptake-time', 'Draft claim 2: uptake time',
  'After the injection the patient waits about 60 minutes before the scan starts, so that the tracer can spread through the body and collect in the tissues that use the most sugar.',
  '60', 'minutes',
  'EANM 2015: 60 min recommended, acceptable range 55 to 75 min. SNM 2006: images typically acquired more than 45 min after injection. FDA label: static images 30 to 100 min after injection. Brain-only scans can start earlier (30 to 50 min).',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006, S.fdgLabel, S.cruk, S.nhs],
  'Draft confirmed (60 min, 55 to 75 min). The 55 to 75 minute window comes from the European guideline and exists to keep uptake measurements (SUV) comparable between scans; it is not a safety limit. For a repeat scan of the same patient the guideline asks for the same waiting time to within 10 minutes.');

add('uptake-rest', 'Draft claim 2: what the patient does during uptake',
  'During the wait the patient sits or lies still in a warm, quiet room and is asked not to talk, because moving, talking and feeling cold all send tracer to muscle or brown fat instead of where the doctors want to look.',
  'seated or lying down, silent, kept warm', '',
  'Same advice in European and US guidelines; for brain scans the room is also dimly lit.',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006, S.radinfo],
  'Added detail, not in the draft. EANM: "the patient should remain seated or recumbent and silent" and "should be kept warm starting 30 to 60 min before the injection" to limit uptake in brown fat. Patients may use the toilet, and are asked to empty the bladder just before the scan.');

// ---------------- 3. Scanning ----------------
add('scan-ct-time', 'Draft claim 3: CT pass',
  'The CT pass comes first and takes less than two minutes.',
  'less than 2', 'minutes',
  'Depends on scanner and scan length; the X-ray beam itself is usually on for well under a minute on a modern multi-slice CT, but the only figure found in a patient-facing professional source is "less than two minutes".',
  [S.radinfo],
  'Draft said "under a minute". CORRECTED to "less than two minutes", the wording of RadiologyInfo.org (RSNA and ACR): "The CT scan takes less than two minutes." No authoritative source was found that states "under a minute" for the whole CT step, so the safer figure is used.');

add('scan-pet-time', 'Draft claim 3: PET pass',
  'The PET pass takes longer, usually about 15 to 30 minutes on a standard scanner, and the patient has to lie still for all of it.',
  '15 to 30', 'minutes',
  'SNM guideline 2006: 15 to 45 min for skull to mid-thigh. RadiologyInfo: PET scan 20 to 30 min, total scanning about 30 min. Cancer Research UK and UCSF: whole scan 30 to 45 min. NHS: 30 to 60 min. A 2021 study timed a routine scan on a current digital scanner (Siemens Biograph Vision 600) at 16 min for 106 cm of body coverage.',
  [S.snm2006, S.radinfo, S.cruk, S.ucsf, S.nhs, S.alberts],
  'Draft said "about 10 to 20 minutes on a modern scanner (older scanners 20 to 45 minutes)". CORRECTED: no authoritative source gives 10 minutes as typical for a standard scanner; the one measured modern figure found is 16 minutes, and current patient leaflets still say 20 to 45 minutes for the whole scan. The older figure is confirmed as 15 to 45 minutes (2006 guideline), not 20 to 45. Scan time depends on patient height and weight, injected activity and scanner sensitivity. Long total-body scanners are much faster (see total-body claims).');

add('scan-range', 'Draft claim 3: body coverage',
  'For most cancer scans the pictures run from the base of the skull to the middle of the thigh, which covers the places where most cancers spread.',
  'base of skull to mid-thigh', '',
  'Extended to the top of the head and to the feet for cancers that often involve the brain, scalp or legs (for example melanoma).',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006],
  'Draft confirmed. EANM calls this "torso imaging" and says it is "standard for both Europe and the US". Patients usually lie with arms raised above the head.');

add('visit-length', 'Draft claim 3: whole visit',
  'The whole visit takes about 2 hours, most of it spent waiting for the tracer to spread.',
  'about 2', 'hours',
  'Cancer Research UK: in the department for around 2 hours. UCSF: the entire procedure takes about two hours. RadiologyInfo: extra tests can lengthen the procedure to three hours.',
  [S.cruk, S.ucsf, S.radinfo],
  'Draft said "about 2 to 3 hours". Narrowed to "about 2 hours" because both sources that give a total say 2 hours; "2 to 3 hours" is still defensible as an allowance (RadiologyInfo mentions three hours when additional tests are done). Sum check: check-in and blood sugar test, about 60 min wait, about 30 min on the scanner.');

// ---------------- 4. Dose ----------------
add('fdg-injected-activity', 'Draft claim 4: injected activity',
  'A typical adult FDG injection contains 185 to 370 MBq of fluorine-18 (5 to 10 millicuries).',
  '185 to 370', 'MBq',
  'FDA label: 5 to 10 mCi (185 to 370 MBq) for adults. European practice scales the activity to body weight and scan time and is often lower. National survey averages collected by UNSCEAR run from 280 to 400 MBq.',
  [S.fdgLabel, S.eanm, S.unscear2020],
  'Draft range confirmed against the FDA label. Unit check (calc.js): 185 MBq = 5 mCi, 370 MBq = 10 mCi. Newer, more sensitive scanners allow lower activities; UNSCEAR notes French units with time-of-flight scanners averaged 3.4 MBq/kg against 4.6 MBq/kg without.');

add('fdg-dose-coefficient', 'Draft claim 4: FDG effective dose',
  'The tracer gives an adult an effective dose of about 0.019 mSv for every MBq injected, so a 185 to 370 MBq injection gives about 3.5 to 7 mSv.',
  '0.019 (so 3.5 to 7.0 mSv for 185 to 370 MBq)', 'mSv/MBq',
  'Adult value. Children get more per MBq (EANM table: 0.024 at 15 years, 0.037 at 10 years, 0.056 at 5 years, 0.095 at 1 year) but are given less activity.',
  [S.eanm, S.snm2006],
  'Draft confirmed. Recomputed (calc.js): 185 x 0.019 = ' + calc.fdgDose_mSv['185 MBq'] + ' mSv; 370 x 0.019 = ' + calc.fdgDose_mSv['370 MBq'] + ' mSv. The coefficient is quoted from ICRP Publication 106 by the EANM guideline ("1.9 x 10^-2 mSv/MBq ... i.e. about 3.5 mSv for an administered activity of 185 MBq") and the same 0.019 appears in the SNM 2006 guideline citing ICRP Publication 80. The ICRP publications themselves were not opened (paywalled); the value was read from the two guidelines that quote them. The organ that receives the most is the bladder wall, which is why patients are told to drink and urinate often.');

add('ct-dose', 'Draft claim 4: CT part of the dose',
  'The CT part adds anywhere from about 1 mSv for the faintest scan used only to correct the PET picture, to 10 to 20 mSv or more for a full diagnostic CT; the low-dose whole-body CT used in most scans added about 3 to 9 mSv in national surveys.',
  '1 to 20 (low-dose protocols in surveys: 2.9 to 8.6)', 'mSv',
  'EANM 2015: "The effective CT dose ranges from 1 to 20 mSv and may be even higher". UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Table D19 low-dose CT component: 2.9 (Germany 2004), 5.9, 6, 6.3, 6.5, 8.2, 8.6 mSv; 13.3 mSv where diagnostic CT was mainly used (Russian Federation 2014 to 2017).',
  [S.eanm, S.unscear2020],
  'Draft said "roughly 1 to 3 mSv for a low-dose CT". CORRECTED: survey data show that the "low-dose" CT actually used in whole-body PET/CT usually adds about 3 to 9 mSv; about 1 mSv is the bottom of the EANM range and applies only to very low-dose attenuation-correction scans. The "up to 10 to 20 mSv for a full diagnostic CT" part is consistent with EANM. The SNM 2006 guideline gave an even wider theoretical range (about 5 to 80 mSv) for older protocols; not recommended for the site.');

add('total-dose', 'Draft claim 4: total dose',
  'A whole-body FDG PET/CT scan typically gives a total effective dose of about 10 to 19 mSv, with about 14 mSv a common figure; older scans that included a full diagnostic CT reached about 25 mSv.',
  'about 14 to 15 typical; 10 to 19 in national surveys; about 25 with full diagnostic CT (2005 German study)', 'mSv',
  'UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Table D19 national totals: 9.9, 12.2, 12.7, 14.1, 14.2, 14.3 and 18.6 mSv (10 to 13 mSv for the Russian Federation 2011 to 2013). UNSCEAR text: "a total procedure dose of 14 mSv is not uncommon" and "a typical effective dose of 15 mSv per procedure". Brix et al. 2005 (four German hospitals, diagnostic contrast CT included): about 25 mSv. Arithmetic limits from the guideline ranges: ' + r(calc.total.total_min, 1) + ' to ' + r(calc.total.total_max, 0) + ' mSv.',
  [S.unscear2020, S.brix, S.eanm],
  'Draft said "about 10 to 25 mSv". Refined: the range is right as an outer envelope, but the upper end (25 mSv) comes from a 2005 study on early scanners with full diagnostic CT, and current survey averages sit between 10 and 19 mSv. Each UNSCEAR table row was re-added (PET part + CT part = total) in calc.js and all seven agree. Newer scanners and total-body scanners can go well below 10 mSv. Effective dose is a population-average risk indicator, not a measured dose to one patient; avoid wording that implies precision.');

add('background-world', 'Draft claim 4: natural background, world',
  'For comparison, natural background radiation gives the average person in the world about 2.4 mSv every year.',
  '2.4', 'mSv per year',
  'Typical range 1 to 13 mSv per year depending on where a person lives; sizeable population groups receive 10 to 20 mSv. Components: radon 1.26, ground 0.48, cosmic 0.39, food and drink 0.29 (sum 2.42).',
  [S.unscear2008],
  'Draft confirmed against the UNSCEAR 2008 Report, Volume I (table of average annual doses: "Total natural 2.4", typical range "1 to 13"; Annex B: "worldwide average annual exposure to natural radiation sources remains at 2.4 mSv").');

add('background-usa', 'Draft claim 4: natural background, USA',
  'In the United States the average person receives about 3.1 mSv a year from natural background radiation, and about 6.2 mSv a year in total once medical scans are included.',
  '3.1 natural; 6.2 total', 'mSv per year',
  'The US natural figure is higher than the world average mainly because of radon. Both figures are from NCRP Report No. 160 (2009, data for 2006).',
  [S.epa, S.nrc],
  'Draft said "about 3 mSv per year in the USA"; confirmed and made exact. EPA: "the average annual radiation dose per person in the U.S. is 6.2 millisieverts (620 millirem)" (source NCRP Report No. 160) and about 48 percent of it comes from medical procedures. NRC: "about 0.62 rem (620 millirem) each year. Half of this dose comes from natural background radiation." Half of 6.2 = ' + calc.background.us_natural_from_half_of_6_2 + ' mSv (calc.js). The NRC page blocked direct download and was read through a fetch tool summary; the EPA page was read directly. NCRP Report 160 itself was not opened (paywalled). A later NCRP report (No. 184, 2019) lowered the medical part for 2016; it was not read, so do not quote a newer total.');

add('dose-in-background-years', 'Draft claim 4: comparison of scan dose with background',
  'A 14 mSv PET/CT scan is roughly what a person receives from natural background radiation in about 6 years at the world average rate, or about 4 to 5 years at the United States rate.',
  '5.8 (world, 2.4 mSv/y); 4.5 (USA, 3.1 mSv/y)', 'years of natural background',
  'For the 10 to 19 mSv survey range: about 4 to 8 years at 2.4 mSv per year. For the FDG part alone (3.5 to 7 mSv): about 1.5 to 3 years.',
  [S.unscear2020, S.unscear2008, S.epa],
  'Derived in calc.js: 14 / 2.4 = ' + calc.background.years_world_for['14 mSv'] + ' years; 14 / 3.1 = ' + calc.background.years_us_for['14 mSv'] + ' years; 10 / 2.4 = ' + calc.background.years_world_for['10 mSv'] + '; 7 / 2.4 = ' + calc.background.years_world_for['7 mSv'] + '; 3.5 / 2.4 = ' + calc.background.years_world_for['3.5 mSv'] + '. This comparison is this project\'s own arithmetic, not a quoted figure, and it compares whole-body averages only.');

// ---------------- 5. Decay and aftercare ----------------
add('f18-decay-11h', 'Draft claim 5: how fast the radioactivity disappears',
  'Fluorine-18 loses half of its radioactivity every 110 minutes, so 11 hours after the injection (six half-lives) only about 1.5% is left from decay alone, and the body removes more through urine.',
  '1.55 (1/64 = 1.56 if the half-life is rounded to 110 min)', '% remaining after 11 hours',
  'Half-life 109.77 min (IAEA nuclear data; FDA labels print 109.7 or 109.8 min). Remaining by decay alone: 68% after 1 h, 47% after 2 h, 22% after 4 h, 10% after 6 h, 3.3% after 9 h, 1.1% after 12 h, 0.011% after 24 h.',
  [S.livechart, S.fdgLabel],
  'Draft arithmetic confirmed (calc.js): 660 min / 109.77 min = ' + r(calc.f18.halfLives_in_11h, 3) + ' half-lives, leaving ' + r(calc.f18.remaining_after_11h_pct_T109_77, 2) + '%; with a rounded 110 min half-life it is exactly 6 half-lives and 1/64 = ' + calc.f18.remaining_after_11h_pct_T110 + '%. Either way "about 1.5%" (or "about 1/64") is correct. Decay alone reaches 1% after ' + r(calc.f18.hours_to_1pct, 1) + ' hours. The body also excretes FDG: the FDA label reports about 20.6% of the dose in the bladder 2 hours after injection, so the true amount left in the body is lower than these decay-only figures. MedlinePlus says the radiation "is gone from your body in about 2 to 10 hours", which is looser than the arithmetic; prefer the calculated wording.');

add('after-scan-advice', 'Draft claim 5: advice after the scan',
  'After the scan patients can eat normally, are told to drink plenty of water and empty the bladder often, and are usually asked to avoid long, close contact with babies, young children and pregnant people for the rest of the day.',
  'rest of the day (UK patient advice); 9 to 12 hours appears in guidance for breastfeeding mothers', '',
  'NHS: avoid spending a long time or having close contact with young children or anyone who is pregnant, "such as for the rest of the day". Cancer Research UK: "for the rest of the day". FDA label: urinate as soon as the scan is finished and as often as possible for at least one hour. Local rules differ and some centers give no restriction.',
  [S.nhs, S.cruk, S.fdgLabel, S.radinfo],
  'Draft said "for some hours"; confirmed, and the two UK patient sources give "the rest of the day". No US patient-facing source with a specific number of hours for general contact was found, so the statement uses "usually" and "the rest of the day". Drinking water matters because the bladder wall is the organ that receives the highest dose.');

// ---------------- 6. Uses ----------------
add('uses-cancer', 'Draft claim 6: main uses (cancer)',
  'Most PET/CT scans are done for cancer: to find a tumor, to see how far it has spread, to check whether treatment is working and to look for cancer that has come back.',
  'about 9 in 10 scans', '',
  'United States 2019 (IMV survey): heart scans 8% and brain scans 3% of PET volume, leaving about 89% that is almost all cancer. UNSCEAR: oncology is "more than 90% of all PET procedures in most countries". A Canadian survey cited by a Lancet Oncology Commission found 80.2%.',
  [S.fdgLabel, S.eanm, S.dotmed, S.unscear2020, S.lancet, S.cruk],
  'Draft "the large majority of scans" confirmed. The 89% is a subtraction (100 - 8 - 3, calc.js), not a figure stated by IMV, and the IMV numbers were read from a trade-press report of the paid survey. Safest site wording: "about 9 in 10" or "the large majority". The FDA label lists the cancers in the approval studies: lung, colorectal, pancreatic, breast, thyroid, melanoma, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.');

add('uses-heart', 'Draft claim 6: main uses (heart)',
  'In the heart, FDG PET shows whether weakened heart muscle is still alive and could recover if its blood supply is restored, and it is used to look for inflammation such as cardiac sarcoidosis; other PET tracers measure blood flow to the heart muscle.',
  'viability; inflammation (cardiac sarcoidosis); blood flow with rubidium-82 or nitrogen-13 ammonia', '',
  'About 8% of US PET scans in 2019 were heart scans, mostly blood-flow (perfusion) scans.',
  [S.fdgLabel, S.jamar, S.sarcoid, S.cardiogen, S.ammonia, S.dotmed],
  'Draft confirmed. FDA label wording for the heart: "identification of left ventricular myocardium with residual glucose metabolism and reversible loss of systolic function in patients with coronary artery disease and left ventricular dysfunction". Sarcoidosis is listed as a major indication in the EANM/SNMMI inflammation guideline (read through a fetch tool summary), and a joint SNMMI-ASNC consensus document (2017) covers FDG PET/CT in cardiac sarcoid; only its title and citation were read. Note that most heart PET scans use perfusion tracers, not FDG.');

add('uses-brain', 'Draft claim 6: main uses (brain)',
  'In the brain, FDG PET helps tell different types of dementia apart by showing which regions use less sugar than normal, and helps find the starting point of seizures in people with epilepsy who are being considered for surgery.',
  'dementia; epilepsy (pre-surgical)', '',
  'About 3% of US PET scans in 2019 were brain scans. Other uses in the European brain guideline: movement disorders such as atypical parkinsonism, encephalitis, brain tumors.',
  [S.guedj, S.fdgLabel, S.dotmed],
  'Draft confirmed. Epilepsy is an FDA-labeled use ("regions of abnormal glucose metabolism associated with foci of epileptic seizures"); dementia is covered by the EANM brain guideline (2022) but is not in the FDA FDG label. Amyloid tracers such as florbetapir are a separate kind of brain PET scan (see tracer claims).');

add('uses-infection-inflammation', 'Draft claim 6: main uses (infection and inflammation)',
  'Because infected and inflamed tissue also uses extra sugar, FDG PET/CT is used to look for hidden infections, the cause of a long unexplained fever, inflamed blood vessels and sarcoidosis.',
  'sarcoidosis; bone and spine infection; fever of unknown origin; spread of infection in the blood; vasculitis', '',
  'Major indications listed in the 2013 EANM/SNMMI guideline: sarcoidosis; peripheral bone osteomyelitis; suspected spinal infection; fever of unknown origin; metastatic infection and high-risk bacteremia; primary evaluation of vasculitides such as giant cell arteritis.',
  [S.jamar, S.eanm],
  'Draft confirmed. The guideline page blocked direct download and was read through a fetch tool summary that quoted the list; treat the exact list as needing a second look before quoting it verbatim. This use is not in the FDA FDG label (off-label in the US) but is established in guidelines. The same sugar uptake is why infection and inflammation can be mistaken for cancer on a scan.');

// ---------------- 7. Scale ----------------
add('scale-usa-scans', 'Draft claim 7: scans per year, USA',
  'In the United States about 2.2 million PET scans were done in 2019, the highest yearly total recorded up to then.',
  '2,200,800 (2019)', 'scans per year',
  'IMV reported growth of about 6% a year from 2013 to 2019 and, in a later report, a 12.2% rise in 2024 over 2023, so the current yearly total is higher than 2.2 million, but no later absolute figure was found in an open source.',
  [S.dotmed, S.imv2025],
  'Draft said "about 2 million"; CORRECTED to 2.2 million with the year 2019. The figure is an estimate from a commercial survey (IMV 2020 PET Imaging Market Summary Report), read as reported by DOTmed HealthCare Business News on March 11, 2020, not from the paid report itself. It counts clinical PET scans on fixed and mobile PET, PET/CT and PET/MR systems. The 2024 growth figure comes from IMV\'s own summary of its 2025 report. Do not extrapolate a 2024 or 2025 total on the site.');

add('scale-usa-scanners', 'Draft claim 7: scanners, USA',
  'The United States has roughly 1,700 PET scanners, about 5 for every million people, and about 2,370 hospitals and clinics offered PET scans in 2019, four in ten of them using a mobile scanner that visits on a truck.',
  '1,680 PET systems (5.2 per million), of which 1,596 PET/CT; 2,370 sites in 2019', 'scanners; sites',
  'UNSCEAR Global Survey (data submitted for the 2009 to 2018 assessment; the table does not give the exact year): United States 1,680 PET systems, 5.2 per million; Denmark 7.4 per million. IMV 2019: 2,370 sites, 60% with fixed units and 40% served by mobile PET.',
  [S.unscear2020, S.dotmed],
  'The draft gave no number. The scanner count is from UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Report, Annex A, Table D33; its exact survey year is not printed, so say "in the 2010s". 1,680 / 5.2 implies a population of ' + r(calc.scale.implied_us_population_millions, 0) + ' million, consistent with 2015 to 2016. Site split recomputed: 60% of 2,370 = ' + r(calc.scale.us_fixed_sites, 0) + ' fixed, 40% = ' + r(calc.scale.us_mobile_sites, 0) + ' mobile (calc.js). "On a truck" is this project\'s plain description of a mobile PET service; the source says mobile services "stop at their facilities for several days each month".');

add('scale-world-scans', 'Draft claim 7: scans per year, worldwide',
  'Nobody keeps an exact worldwide count, but United Nations figures suggest several million PET scans a year, roughly 7 million, with about a third of them in the United States.',
  'about 6.8 million (derived: 17% of 40 million), period 2009 to 2018', 'scans per year',
  'Very uncertain. UNSCEAR gives its nuclear medicine totals an uncertainty of tens of percent, and the 17% PET share comes from the countries that answered its survey (range 1% to 67% between countries).',
  [S.unscear2020],
  'The draft gave no number. This is a DERIVED estimate, not a quoted one: UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Report (Annex A) assesses "the total number of procedures worldwide in diagnostic nuclear medicine (including PET)" as 40 million a year for 2009 to 2018 and says PET procedures "now represent 17% of all nuclear medicine procedures"; 40 million x 0.17 = ' + r(calc.scale.world_pet_estimate / 1e6, 1) + ' million (calc.js). The US 2019 figure (2.2 million) would be ' + r(calc.scale.us_share_of_world_estimate_pct, 0) + '% of that. Market-research sites quote 3 to 5 million, which looks too low against the US figure alone and was not used. If the site wants zero risk, say "several million a year" and drop the specific 7 million.');

add('scale-world-scanners', 'Draft claim 7: scanners, worldwide',
  'PET scanners are spread very unevenly: the International Atomic Energy Agency found about one PET/CT scanner for every 600,000 people in high-income countries, against one for every 167 million people in low-income countries.',
  'no authoritative worldwide total found; 1 per about 601,000 people (high income) to 1 per about 166,667,000 (low income)', 'people per PET/CT scanner',
  'IAEA IMAGINE database as analyzed by Gallach et al. 2020: 601,000 (high income), 3,484,000 (upper-middle), 10,000,000 (lower-middle), 166,667,000 (low income). UNSCEAR: 7 of 49 surveyed countries had no PET at all. Lancet Oncology Commission (IMAGINE data): mean 3.6 PET scanners per million people in high-income countries, 0.3 in upper-middle-income countries.',
  [S.gallach, S.unscear2020, S.lancet],
  'NOT RESOLVED: no primary or authoritative source with a worldwide total number of PET or PET/CT scanners could be read. The IAEA IMAGINE database holds country figures but only as an interactive dashboard that could not be downloaded, and its data date from about 2019 to 2020. Do not print a world total on the site. The per-person figures are from an IAEA-authored paper (Medical Science Monitor 2020) and are averages by World Bank income group. The Lancet Commission table has internal oddities (the stated mean exceeds the stated upper quartile), so quote it with care or not at all.');

// ---------------- 8. Total-body PET ----------------
add('totalbody-length', 'Draft claim 8: total-body PET, length',
  'The uEXPLORER scanner, built by a team at the University of California, Davis with United Imaging Healthcare in Shanghai, has a detector tunnel 194 cm long, enough to image the whole body of more than 99% of adults at once.',
  '194', 'cm (axial field of view)',
  'A standard PET/CT scanner covers about 15 to 30 cm at a time (the one in the 2021 comparison study covers 26.3 cm) and moves the patient through in steps. Another long scanner, the Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra, covers 106 cm.',
  [S.badawi, S.spencer, S.alberts],
  'Draft confirmed: "The 194-cm axial field of view of the EXPLORER PET/CT scanner is sufficient to cover, for the first time, the entire human adult body in a single acquisition in more than 99% of the population" (Badawi et al., J Nucl Med 2019). The first human studies were published in 2019; Spencer et al. 2021 call uEXPLORER "the first commercially available total-body PET scanner". Only the abstracts and author affiliations of these papers were read (full text not open through the API). 194 / 26.3 = ' + r(calc.explorer.ratio_to_26_3cm, 1) + ' times the coverage of that standard scanner (calc.js). The "15 to 30 cm" for standard scanners is general knowledge and should be checked against the instrumentation batch.');

add('totalbody-sensitivity', 'Draft claim 8: total-body PET, sensitivity',
  'Because its detectors surround the whole body, a total-body scanner catches far more of the gamma rays, and its designers calculated a gain of about 40 times for whole-body imaging compared with a standard scanner.',
  'about 40 (whole body); about 4 to 5 (single organ)', 'times the effective sensitivity',
  'The factor of about 40 is a design estimate published in 2018 before the scanner was finished. The measured sensitivity of the finished scanner is 174 kcps/MBq (NEMA NU 2-2018 test).',
  [S.cherry, S.spencer],
  'Draft confirmed with a caveat. Source wording (Cherry et al., J Nucl Med 2018): "by increasing the geometric coverage to encompass the entire body, sensitivity can be increased by a factor of about 40 for total-body imaging or a factor of about 4 to 5 for imaging a single organ such as the brain or heart". Present it as "about 40 times" or "up to about 40 times" for whole-body scans and say it is a calculated figure; do not say "40 times better pictures". Abstracts only were read.');

add('totalbody-fast-low-dose', 'Draft claim 8: total-body PET, speed and dose',
  'The extra sensitivity can be spent in different ways: the first human studies showed usable whole-body pictures from scans of about 1 minute or less, or from an injection of only 25 MBq, less than a tenth of a usual dose.',
  'about 1 minute or less; 25 MBq or less', '',
  'Initial case studies (2019), not routine practice. A 2021 patient study on a 106 cm scanner matched a 16-minute standard scan in under 2 minutes.',
  [S.badawi, S.alberts],
  'Draft confirmed. Source wording (Badawi et al. 2019): "the sensitivity gain can be used to acquire diagnostic PET images with very small amounts of activity in the field of view (25 MBq, 0.7 mCi or less), with very short acquisition times (about 1 min or less) or at later time points". The authors call this "initial evidence". Arithmetic (calc.js): 25 MBq x 0.019 = ' + calc.fdgDose_mSv['25 MBq'] + ' mSv from the tracer, and 370 / 25 = ' + calc.explorer.dose_ratio_370_over_25 + ', so "less than a tenth of a usual dose" holds for usual doses above 250 MBq; against the lowest label dose (185 MBq) it is about one seventh, so "a small fraction" is the wording that is true in every case. The same scanner can also film the tracer moving through the whole body with frames as short as 1 second.');
